concept.name: Reproducible analysis
concept.definition: An analysis whose results can be independently regenerated from the same data, code, and documented procedure. The U.S. National Academies (2019) distinguish reproducibility — obtaining consistent results using the same input data, computational steps, methods, and code — from replicability, obtaining consistent results across studies aimed at the same question with new data.
concept.intuition: Someone else (or you, six months later) should be able to rerun the pipeline from the recorded inputs and get the same numbers — otherwise the result is a story, not a finding.
concept.mechanics: Reproducibility is engineered by pinning data versions, code, parameters, random seeds, and environments; recording provenance of every artifact; and automating the pipeline so re-execution is one command. Reports declare assumptions, costs, and evaluation splits so results can be checked rather than trusted.
concept.failure_modes: Silent dependencies break reproduction: unpinned library or data versions, hidden manual steps, nondeterministic components (including LLM calls at nonzero temperature), and lookahead-prone data handling that cannot be reconstructed later. Vendor data that is revised retroactively (e.g., restated fundamentals) makes past inputs unrecoverable unless snapshotted.
concept.misconceptions: Reproducibility is not a claim that the result is correct — a wrong analysis can be perfectly reproducible, and a true finding can be irreproducibly presented. 'The code is available' is not enough if the data and environment are not.
concept.example: A backtest report ships with the exact data snapshot, commit hash, parameter file, and seed; a reviewer reruns it and regenerates the identical equity curve and drawdown statistics before the strategy is discussed further.

citations.source: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 'Reproducibility and Replicability in Science' (2019)
